name: Mental accounting
statement: People sort money into separate mental accounts by source and purpose, then spend from each as though the balances could not be moved between them.
meaning: Money is fungible. A pound of salary and a pound of lottery winnings buy the same bread, and standard consumer theory says only the total matters. Mental accounting says households keep books instead. Thaler's 1999 review sets out three components. The first covers how outcomes are perceived and experienced, using the prospect theory value function to code gains and losses. The second is the assignment of activities to accounts, so that housing, food and entertainment carry their own budgets. The third is how often accounts are evaluated, daily or yearly, narrowly or broadly. Thaler's abstract says each component violates fungibility. That structure is the reason the idea is hard to test as a whole. Mental accounting is a framework generating many separate predictions, and the evidence for them is uneven. Some hold in field data on real money. Others do not survive a well-powered repeat of the original question.

origin.note: "Mental Accounting and Consumer Choice" ran in Marketing Science 4(3), 199-214. Its abstract describes a model that starts from the mental coding of gains and losses using the prospect theory value function, then values purchases through the new concept of transaction utility, then folds in the household budgeting process. The name is older than the model. Kahneman and Tversky's 1984 American Psychologist paper uses "mental account" throughout and says its analysis "owes a large debt to the stimulating work of Richard Thaler (1980, in press), who showed the relevance of this process to consumer behavior". Thaler's 1999 Journal of Behavioral Decision Making review is the version later work replicates against.

evidence: The founding demonstrations are hypothetical questions. Kahneman and Tversky put two theatre problems to separate groups in 1984. In Problem 8, N = 200, respondents had paid $10 for a ticket and lost it at the door; 46 percent said they would buy another and 54 percent said they would not. In Problem 9, N = 183, they had lost a $10 bill on the way in; 88 percent said they would still buy a ticket. The cash loss is not posted to the account for the play, so it does not raise the felt cost of seeing it. The same paper reports a second case. Sixty-eight percent of 88 respondents would drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 calculator, while 29 percent of 93 would make the same trip to save $5 on a $125 one. Li and Feldman trace both problems to Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 Science paper. The house-money evidence is separate, and part of it used real stakes. Thaler and Johnson ran their Experiment 4 in a large introductory economics class at Cornell, where roughly 98 percent of students agreed to take part for money. After a prior gain of $15 shown apart from the gamble, 77 percent of 95 subjects took the risky option; under the one-stage wording, 44 percent of 111 did. Their hypothetical versions gave 70 to 82 percent risk seeking in the two-stage form against 43 to 44 percent in the one-stage form. The 70 percent that later reviews quote is one row of their Table 5: 44 Cornell MBA students told they had just won $30. Thaler and Johnson also describe an independent replication by Battalio, Kagel and Komain, in which 21 of 35 subjects, 60 percent, took a comparable gamble after a $30 endowment. Field tests came later and mostly test the labelling claim rather than the house-money one. Hastings and Shapiro used a panel of gasoline purchases at a grocery retailer. Milkman and Beshears tracked what online grocery customers did with a $10 discount. Abeler and Marklein ran a German restaurant study and a laboratory experiment on labelled budgets. Hastings and Shapiro's later work on food stamps puts the marginal propensity to consume eligible food out of SNAP benefits at 0.5 to 0.6, calls the propensity out of cash much smaller, and rejects the hypothesis that households respect fungibility.

replication.headline: A registered replication of the 17 problems in Thaler's review supported 11, the house-money problem came out backwards, and a meta-analysis of that effect falls to nothing once publication bias is corrected.
replication.detail: Li and Feldman ran a preregistered replication of every problem reviewed in Thaler 1999, with about 500 participants per problem and 1,007 in total. They found support for 11 of the 17, mixed support for three and no support for three. Four further predictions Thaler stated without evidence were tested as extensions, of which two were supported. The theatre-ticket problem is among the successes, and its numbers moved. In the lost-cash condition, 90 percent of 252 would buy a ticket, against 88 percent originally. In the lost-ticket condition, 77 percent of 251 would buy another, against 46 percent originally. Cramer's V for the contrast fell from 0.44, 95% CI [0.34, 0.54], to 0.17, 95% CI [0.09, 0.27]. The calculator problem failed outright: 11 percent would drive for the $15 calculator and 7 percent for the $125 one, giving Cramer's V of 0.07, 95% CI [0.00, 0.17], with a chi-square of 3.39 on one degree of freedom and p = 0.066. The house-money problem reversed. Told they had just won $30, 28 percent of 504 took a 50-50 bet on $9, against 70 percent in Thaler's review, giving Cohen's h of -0.46, 95% CI [-0.54, -0.37], against an original h of 0.41. The two prior-loss problems parted company. The plain version, where a prior loss offers no route back to even, was supported, with 17 percent risk seeking against 40 percent originally. The break-even version, offering a 33 percent chance of $30 against a sure $10, reversed: 24 percent took the gamble against 60 percent originally, giving Cohen's h of -0.55, 95% CI [-0.63, -0.46]. Dan's meta-analysis of the house-money effect pooled 36 studies, 57 continuous effect sizes and 18 binary ones. The continuous pooled estimate is g = 0.37, 95% CI [0.22, 0.51], with I-squared of 88.1 percent and a prediction interval from -0.61 to 1.35. Egger's test found asymmetry, intercept 2.92, 95% CI [1.86, 3.98], p < 0.0001, and trim-and-fill brings the estimate to g = 0.07, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.25]. Split by design, questionnaires give 0.51 and laboratory studies 0.43, both at p < 0.01, while field experiments give 0.17 and do not reach the 5 percent level. Studies published before 2009 give 0.64 and those after 2020 give 0.18. The field record on labelling runs the other way. Hastings and Shapiro estimate that a $1 rise in the petrol price raises a household's propensity to buy regular grade by 0.0142, standard error 0.0010, while a $1,000 rise in total expenditure lowers it by 0.0008. The Wald test of equality has a p-value printed as 0.0000. They write that the marginal utility of money "increases 15 times more in response to an increase in the gasoline price than in response to an equivalent decrease in income from other sources". The same specification applied to milk and orange juice brands cannot reject fungibility. Abeler and Marklein gave restaurant guests 8-euro vouchers across 22 days and 187 tables. Guests whose voucher was labelled for beverages spent 18.55 euros per person on drinks, 3.84 more than guests given a voucher good for the whole bill. In their laboratory version, subjects given an in-kind grant bought 16.6 units of the targeted good against 14.4 in the cash condition, where 13 was optimal, and 21 percent spent the whole grant on the targeted good against 1 percent under cash. Milkman and Beshears found that redeeming a $10 coupon raised an online grocery order by $1.59, standard error 0.79 clustered by customer, on an average order of $150.23.

study.cite: Li, M., & Feldman, G. (2025). Revisiting mental accounting classic paradigms: Replication Registered Report of the problems reviewed in Thaler (1999). Royal Society Open Science, 12(9), 250979.

limits: The strongest field results test one narrow claim: that money carrying a label is spent differently from money that does not. They do not test the framework's other components. Hastings and Shapiro's petrol sample is selective by construction. It keeps households buying gasoline at the retailer at least 24 times in each of 2006, 2007 and 2008, and the paper says the majority of gasoline-buying households are therefore excluded. The estimation sample is 61,494 households out of 1,306,748 in the retailer's data. Those retained live 4.100 miles from their most visited store against 20.579 miles for all retailer households, and spent $2,554 on groceries in 2008 against $506. Searches of Crossref, Europe PMC and the open web on 21 September 2026 found no published re-analysis or independent replication of that gasoline result. Abeler and Marklein describe their field study as suggestive rather than conclusive, and it was not randomised day by day: the restaurant "first issued all beverage vouchers", and bill vouchers followed from the next day, because the owner feared daily switching would confuse the waiters. Their figures here come from the accepted manuscript of July 2015 in the Oxford University Research Archive, since the published article answered with a bot challenge. Milkman and Beshears' coupon coefficient clears the 5 percent level and no more, and their figures here come from the 2008 working paper rather than the 2009 journal article, which sits behind Elsevier. Dan's meta-analysis prints two versions of several numbers. The abstract gives a pooled risk ratio of 1.33, which is the estimate after two outliers are removed, while the general binary analysis gives 1.46, 95% CI [1.27, 1.69]. The forest-plot caption gives g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.22, 0.55], where the results text gives 0.37, 95% CI [0.22, 0.51]. The figures above are the ones in the results text. Li and Feldman's sample was drawn from Amazon Mechanical Turk in the United States through CloudResearch, and every problem they tested is hypothetical.
misreadings: The lost-ticket percentages are quoted as if they were constants. In 1984 the gap between the two conditions was 42 points. In 2025, with about 250 people per condition, it was 13, because the share willing to replace a lost ticket rose from 46 to 77 percent. The direction survives and the size does not. Kahneman and Tversky flagged a second instability in the same paper: willingness to replace a lost ticket rose when that problem followed the lost-cash version, while the reverse order changed nothing. Seeing both makes the inconsistency visible, and only in one direction. The calculator problem is still taught as a demonstration of topical accounts and no longer produces one. Li and Feldman report a participant's remark that driving 20 minutes now costs more than $5, then say the exact reason for the different findings is down to speculation. The house-money effect is the claim most often stated without qualification. Prior gains raise risk-taking in questionnaires and laboratories, and the pooled effect shrinks as the setting approaches the real world. Flepp and Rüdisser used slot-machine records from 5,169 players at a real casino and report that players wager less after hitting a jackpot, with jackpot size adding nothing. Their abstract is all this entry could obtain, so no coefficient from it is quoted here. A second error is arithmetical. Hastings and Shapiro's two coefficients are often divided into each other to yield a ratio of about 20; the paper's own comparison is that the marginal utility of money moves 15 times more with the petrol price than with income from elsewhere. The deepest error is treating mental accounting as a single effect with a single verdict. It is a framework, and evidence for one prediction is not evidence for the others. Several of its parts carry their own records here: sunk cost, entry 1, framing, entry 7, loss aversion, entry 31, the endowment effect, entry 46, the denomination effect, entry 178, and the disposition effect, entry 209. Hastings and Shapiro's own placebo test makes the point: households that violated fungibility at the petrol pump obeyed it when choosing brands of milk and orange juice.

Thaler, R. H. (1999). Mental accounting matters. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 12(3), 183-206. Read from a scan of the published article; the three prior-outcome problems and their percentages sit on page 198.
Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1984). Choices, values, and frames. American Psychologist, 39(4), 341-350. Source of the theatre-ticket and calculator problems and their percentages.

Thaler, R. H., & Johnson, E. J. (1990). Gambling with the house money and trying to break even: The effects of prior outcomes on risky choice. Management Science, 36(6), 643-660. Read in full as the published article, from a JSTOR scan hosted by Columbia Business School. An SSRN delivery link to a submitted version answered with a Cloudflare bot challenge, so the published copy was used instead.
